title: The Book of Scion, Chapter 1
summary: With the news today that Toyota has resurrected Scion as “a new brand built around curiosity, possibility, and the freedom to explore mobility in new ways,” via a trio of very different vehicles to kick off this next chapter, we thought it might be beneficial to flip back a few pages and revisit the prologue […]
body_markdown:
With the news today that Toyota has resurrected Scion as “a new brand built around curiosity, possibility, and the freedom to explore mobility in new ways,” via[a trio of very different vehicles](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/a-u-s-market-kei-truck-with-a-scion-badge-its-happening/) to kick off this next chapter, we thought it might be beneficial to flip back a few pages and revisit the prologue and first chapter of the Japanese carmaker’s funky ancillary brand.


By the late 1990s, Toyota was desperate to capture the early millennials who were coming of age, coming into some money, and already showing their disdain for beige Tercels, tan Corollas, and gold Camrys. Project Genesis, launched in 1999, was designed to do just that, with an emphasis on marketing the third-generation MR-2, seventh-gen Celica, and the Echo together as youthful alternatives. By 2001, without the response it had hoped for, Toyota nixed the project.


Undeterred, and with plenty of valuable knowledge gained from what had worked and what hadn’t, Toyota then launched Project Exodus, the undertaking that would become Scion. That word, in retrospect, was fitting, for “the descendant from a notable family” was exactly what Scion would become.


AFP via Getty Images


AFP via Getty Images


Toyota introduced the bbX (left) and ccX concepts at the New York auto show in 2002.


Toyota introduced[its new brand](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/our-two-cents-9-automotive-brands-we-miss/) in March 2002 at the New York International Auto Show, with the bbX and ccX concepts, both of which would morph into production models as the xB and tC, respectively. Later that year, at SEMA, Toyota displayed a mock Scion dealership space, which was hip and trendy and not at all like the Buick-y feel of its own showrooms. Novel beyond just the décor, however, would be the sales pitch: The cars would come in a single trim, with a ton of options to let the kids customize their funky little rides any which way they chose. Scion Pure Price, meanwhile, was a fixed, no-haggle price tag, with the showrooms devoid of lingering salespeople; they were instructed only to approach when it was clear they were wanted. And each car came with Scion Service Boost, a free two-year maintenance program that preceded its parent company’s own such program, ToyotaCare, by seven years.


At the 2003 Los Angeles Auto show, Scion unveiled its first production cars, the xA subcompact hatchback, based on the Toyota Ist sold in Japan, and the xB, which was derived from the Japanese Toyota bB. Both were powered by Toyota’s 108-horsepower 1.5-liter four-cylinder, with a choice of five-speed manual or four-speed automatic. The xB has been classified as a subcompact hatchback, an MPV, an SUV, a minivan, a toaster, and more, but the truth is the xB came to define a segment of small, tall, boxy, little van-like things here in the U.S. that would eventually include the Kia Soul and Nissan Cube.


Toyota


Toyota


The fledgling brand sold nearly 11,000 cars in its first year and just shy of 100,000 in 2004, when it also began a program called Release Series, or RS. These were essentially limited-edition models, often in wild colors such as Hot Lava Orange, Solar Yellow, Maziora Torched Penny, and Spectra Blue, decked out with exclusive options, and the whole series was designed to create buzz, which it did. Most of the brand’s 1004 nationwide dealerships would only get a few of each RS model.


The handsome tC joined the lineup in 2005, with the sporty look of a coupe and the practicality of a hatchback, and sales of Scion’s three-car lineup topped 156,000. The tC was an instant hit, but the xB had become the brand’s darling, and it accounted for more than 61,000 of the 173,000 total sales in 2006, Scion’s pinnacle in the market.


Toyota


Scion redesigned the xB for 2008, making it wider, longer, larger, heavier, and rounder overall, with 50 extra horses, too, from its 2.4-liter four-cylinder, but it failed to capture the magic of the original’s JDM-ness, while the xA was replaced by the similar xD.


The 2008 financial crisis hit millennials, and Scion as a result, particularly hard, and sales began to fall precipitously, to 58,000 in 2009 and less than 46,000 in 2010.


Scion


Toyota


Toyota


The diminutive 2012 iQ did nothing to better the situation, and the second-gen tC never really landed, either. The rear-wheel-drive 2013 FR-S, however, was[a revelation](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-original-scion-fr-s-subaru-brz-is-the-millennial-generations-datsun-240z/) : Here was a fun, great-looking, entry-level, dopamine hit of a coupe, developed jointly with Subaru, that gave Scion a hopeful boost once again. Only to be undone somewhat in 2015 by the uninspiring, Mazda 2-based iA sedan and the iM, a Corolla hatchback in disguise. Neither model screamed “youthful” or “exciting.”


Toyota announced in early 2016 that it had the plug on its “test laboratory division,” after nearly 1.1 million Scions had been sold. But, as we’ve just seen with the announcement of the KEI-01, along with the SxS and BKE concepts, it wasn’t a plug-pulling, after all. Toyota had simply dog-eared the page and set the book down for a while. Experimental mobility seems to be the next chapter in the Scion book, one we will happily keep reading.
